title: Results, goals and an honest look at your working day

say: Results, goals, and an honest look at your working day.
This is the video for Module 1 of Productivity and Time Management at Work.
Ask people how their week went, and many will say, very busy. Busy describes activity: messages answered, calls taken, meetings attended.

say: Productivity describes output. For a caterer, that is orders delivered on time and paid for.

say: And before you change anything, you will measure how your day is really spent.

panel.heading: Busy is not the same as productive

Measure where your time really goes

say: Every role has three to five key results areas, the few outcomes that make everything else easier. Write them as results, not tasks.
Most key results depend on deep work. That is focused, demanding work that needs your experience and judgement, like writing a proposal or preparing a budget.
Shallow work is easier, like forwarding a file. If a smart new colleague could do it well after one week of training, it is probably shallow.
Shallow work arrives all day by itself. Deep work only happens if you protect time for it.
Amaka works from 8 in the morning to 8 at night, but profit is flat.
She lists everything she did on Tuesday. 14 tasks, including 3 hours on WhatsApp.
She writes her results areas, such as jobs delivered on time, new corporate clients, and cash collected. Only 5 of the 14 tasks served a result. None served new clients.
So every weekday from 9 to 10:30 is now for deep work on one results area. Within the week she sends her company profile to 6 potential clients, work she had postponed for months while staying busy.
A goal turns a results area into a target with a finish line. A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant to your results, and has a deadline.
Improve customer service is vague. Reply to every WhatsApp enquiry within 2 working hours is SMART.

say: An OKR is an objective plus key results. The objective is what you want, in plain inspiring words, with no number.

say: The common mistake is measuring effort. Send 50 flyers is an activity. Get 10 new office enquiries is a result.

panel.rule: A key result measures an outcome, not an activity

say: Her sales have been uneven. Her objective: build steady monthly sales from returning customers.
Key result 1. 40 repeat customers by 30 September. Her sales book shows about 15 last quarter. That is her baseline.
Key result 2. An average order of 25000 naira or more, up from about 18000.
Key result 3. 4 new collections announced on schedule.
Now every Friday she checks three numbers, instead of a general hope for more sales.
Now measure your starting point, your baseline. For 3 normal days, record what you worked on in 30-minute blocks, or each time you switch task.

panel.heading: Log 3 working days
items: Note the results area, deep or shallow
Tally interruptions: W, E, C, P, S

say: Note which results area it served, and whether it was deep or shallow.

panel.heading: Log 3 working days
items: Note the results area, deep or shallow
Tally interruptions: W, E, C, P, S

say: Tally every interruption with a letter. W for WhatsApp, E for email, C for calls, P for a person, and S for self, like picking up your phone just to check.

panel.heading: Log 3 working days
items: Note the results area, deep or shallow
Tally interruptions: W, E, C, P, S

say: Then count focused deep-work hours, with zero or one interruption.

panel.heading: Log 3 working days
items: Note the results area, deep or shallow
Tally interruptions: W, E, C, P, S

say: Funke feels she never has time to write donor reports. She logs 3 days.
She gets only 1 focused hour a day, and 23 interruptions a day. 31 of them in three days came from WhatsApp, mostly a busy staff group chat.
54 percent of her time goes on results.
She has 2 hours of meetings a day, so 6 hours left. Minus a 20 percent buffer for the unexpected, she can plan about 4.8 hours.
Do not plan to 100 percent. The first urgent request would break the whole day.
To remember. Measure yourself by output. Protect time for deep work. Write key results as outcomes with numbers and dates.
Tally interruptions by source, and plan only to your real capacity, with a buffer.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Measure yourself by output, not activity
Plan to real capacity, with a buffer

say: Now your turn. Write your key results areas, write one OKR for this quarter, and run your three-day baseline. Keep your numbers for Module 4.
